title: THEY LAUGHED WHEN PAUL SAID THE DEAD WOULD RISE—THEN SOMETHING HAPPENED IN ATHENS
paragraphs: THEY LAUGHED WHEN PAUL SAID THE DEAD WOULD RISE—THEN SOMETHING HAPPENED IN ATHENS

Athens had philosophers, temples, arguments, idols, and intellectual prestige. Then one scarred Christian stood before them and proclaimed the one truth sophisticated people could not comfortably absorb: Jesus Christ had risen from the dead—and if the tomb was really empty, nobody listening could remain neutral forever.
Think about that for a moment.
Not because Paul forgot what he wanted to say.
Not because someone proved that Jesus was still lying in a grave.
They laughed when the message reached the resurrection.
Acts records the moment with almost painful simplicity:
“Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked.”
In the Greek text, the words are:
οἱ μὲν ἐχλεύαζον — hoi men echleuazon
There is something chillingly modern about that sentence.
Nearly two thousand years have passed, yet you can almost hear the laughter.
You can hear it in the university classroom.
You can hear it in the comment section.
You can hear it among friends when somebody begins talking seriously about Jesus.
You can even hear it inside your own mind when Christianity stops being inspirational language and begins making supernatural claims.
A crucified Man physically raised from death?
A God who cannot be reduced to whatever version of spirituality makes us comfortable?
That was where Paul's audience had to decide what they were actually hearing.
Because Christianity does not finally stand before humanity saying, “Here are some principles that might improve your life.”
And if that announcement is true, everything changes.
But before the laughter came, Paul had walked through Athens.
This was Athens—the city whose name still echoes through the history of philosophy, art, politics, literature, and intellectual achievement.
Yet Acts tells us that when Paul looked around, his spirit was deeply provoked because the city was full of idols.
Paul did not look at brilliant people and hate them.
He looked at worshipers searching in the wrong places and his heart burned.
That is an important distinction for Christians living in an unbelieving world.
Paul was not frightened by intelligent questions.
He did not hide from philosophers.
He did not retreat into a Christian bubble and complain that Athens had become too secular.
He went where the people were.
Eventually Epicurean and Stoic philosophers began engaging him.
The underlying Greek word is σπερμολόγος — spermologos, literally carrying the image of a seed-picker, and by extension someone thought to be picking up scraps of ideas and passing them around.
Paul had encountered the risen Christ.
He had suffered for preaching Christ.
His entire life had been overturned by Christ.
And sophisticated men effectively looked at him and said:
Because when you know the Gospel is not merely your opinion, ridicule loses some of its power.
That does not mean ridicule stops hurting.
Some of you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe you started taking Jesus seriously and suddenly people thought you had become strange.
Maybe your friends tolerate spirituality but become uncomfortable when you say the name Jesus.
Maybe people applaud “finding yourself” but become uneasy when you talk about denying yourself, taking up your cross, repenting of sin, and following Christ.
Maybe you have learned to keep your faith quiet because you remember what happened the last time you spoke.
The accusation that Christianity is outdated.
And slowly, almost without noticing, you began editing Jesus so people would accept you.
Paul also did not enter Athens screaming insults at Athenians.
He understood enough about their world to speak into it.
Then he was brought to the Areopagus.
And there, surrounded by people fascinated with new ideas, Paul began not with contempt but with a point of contact.
He had noticed an altar bearing an inscription:
The One you worship without knowing, I am proclaiming to you.
Paul tells these people that the God who made the world cannot be contained inside human temples as though humanity could construct a house large enough for its Creator.
God does not depend upon human hands.
The Athenians were surrounded by objects humans had made for gods.
Paul announced the God who made humans.
The Gospel begins somewhere far more humbling:
“What could you possibly give the God who gave you your next breath?”
And suddenly Athens doesn't feel ancient anymore.
Our idols simply became harder to recognize.
An idol does not have to be a statue.
Anything we treat as ultimate, anything from which we demand the identity, security, worth, satisfaction, or salvation that belongs to God alone can begin occupying sacred territory inside the heart.
And perhaps the most dangerous idols are the ones we never call idols.
And then comes one of the most tender truths spoken in the entire confrontation:
God “is not far from each one of us.”
Maybe that sentence is why you are still reading.
Because perhaps you have felt very far from Him.
Maybe there is something on your phone nobody knows about.
Maybe your marriage is quietly bleeding.
Maybe you smile in church while privately wondering whether God has finally become tired of you.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary but your prayer life has almost disappeared.
Maybe you once burned for Jesus and now you barely recognize the person you have become.
Maybe you are not an atheist.
And somewhere beneath all of that, you wonder:
“After everything I've done… how far away is God?”
But do not confuse His nearness with approval of everything we do.
Because Paul's sermon does not end with a comforting spiritual embrace.
And this is where modern Christianity is often tempted to stop reading.
νῦν παραγγέλλει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις πάντας πανταχοῦ μετανοεῖν
The force of Paul's statement is unmistakable:
God now commands people everywhere to repent.
Not merely to post a Bible verse.
Not merely to agree that Jesus existed.
Repentance involves a genuine turning—a changed orientation toward God that bears fruit in life.
And that is where the Gospel wounds before it heals.
Because grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
There was judgment borne by Christ.
The Son of God did not enter human history because humanity needed motivational improvement.
Paul himself was living evidence of that scandalous grace.
Before Paul became the missionary mocked for Christ, Saul had persecuted followers of Christ.
He had entered houses and dragged believers away.
The man standing in Athens preaching Jesus had once tried to crush the movement bearing Jesus' name.
If Christianity were merely a story about good people earning God's acceptance, Paul's biography would be an embarrassment.
Instead, Paul's biography became a trophy of mercy.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence if your life is surrendered to Christ.
Your sin may explain wounds in your story.
It does not have to become the title of your eternity.
The religious person hiding secret sin can repent.
The skeptic can come to Christ.
The person reading this while thinking, “If Christians knew the real me, they wouldn't want me,” can come.
But we do not come negotiating the terms.
And Paul told Athens why repentance was urgent.
God has appointed a day of righteous judgment.
Then Paul said God had given assurance concerning the appointed Man by raising Him from the dead.
The moment Christianity refused to remain a pleasant philosophical conversation.
Luke does not give us a psychological profile of each person, so we should not pretend to know every motive.
But the text clearly shows that the resurrection produced divided responses.
Others said they wanted to hear Paul again.
And maybe those same three responses are sitting behind screens right now.
Somebody reading this thinks the whole thing is ridiculous.
Somebody else feels something stirring but says:
Later when following Jesus costs less.
And somebody else has reached the place where excuses are becoming exhausting.
You know how to look okay.
And here is the terrifying thing about “later”:
Paul did not tell Athens that repentance was an interesting option to consider when convenient.
He proclaimed Christ in light of resurrection and coming judgment.
Yet Christianity's message of judgment cannot be separated from Christianity's message of rescue.
The Judge is the One who stretched out His hands upon a cross.
Jesus did not remain safely distant from human rebellion.
And on the third day, the Christian proclamation declares that death lost its prisoner.
The stone did not keep Him.
The grave did not finish Him.
This is why the resurrection cannot be reduced to a metaphor for “starting over.”
The apostles proclaimed it as something God actually did.
Paul later made the stakes explicit in 1 Corinthians 15: if Christ has not been raised, Christian faith collapses.
Christianity itself places enormous weight upon this claim.
That means Christians should never fear sincere investigation.
Look at what Christianity actually claims rather than what somebody on social media says it claims.
But do not dismiss Jesus merely because resurrection sounds impossible.
Of course resurrection sounds impossible if death has the final authority.
The Christian claim is not that dead people naturally get back up.
The claim is that God raised Jesus.
And Acts 17 tells us that after the mocking, something quieter happened.
No dramatic record of the entire city converting.
No description of thousands rushing forward.
I love that Scripture remembers their names.
But heaven was not measuring the success of Paul's sermon by the volume of the laughter.
Never forget that when you share Jesus.
You may post truth and receive almost nothing.
But somewhere there may be a Damaris reading silently.
Somewhere there may be a Dionysius whose heart is cracking open.
Someone may never comment, but tonight they might pray for the first time in years.
You do not know what God may do with one faithful witness.
So do not be ashamed of Christ.
And do not confuse being mocked with being defeated.
The resurrection did not become less true because someone laughed.
Truth does not require applause to remain truth.
And perhaps that is the word somebody desperately needs today.
You have been allowing the crowd to determine how loudly you love Jesus.
You have been measuring obedience by reactions.
You have been hiding convictions because you fear losing approval.
Remember Paul standing among the philosophers.
He did not need to prove he was the smartest man in Athens.
He needed to faithfully proclaim Christ.
Neither do you need to win every argument.
You need to belong to Jesus.
And before you think about the unbeliever who needs this article, allow Scripture to turn its light toward you.
What has your heart begun worshiping?
What would Jesus ask you to surrender that makes you instinctively reach for an excuse?
Maybe the real scandal is not that Athens had idols.
Maybe the scandal is how easily Christians can have them too.
And Jesus does not expose idols because He delights in humiliating you.
He exposes what is killing you because He calls you away from false gods and back to the living God.
Grace that does not merely cover yesterday but begins rewriting tomorrow.
Grace that can take a persecutor named Saul and turn him into a preacher named Paul.
Grace that can enter your scandal and refuse to leave you there.
So if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, don't hide.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to make Christ willing to receive repentant sinners.
You need Christ because you cannot save yourself.
Maybe your prayer tonight is nothing impressive.
Salvation is not measured by emotional intensity.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
But sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is the first public crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And when you see somebody else write those words, don't treat their vulnerability like content.
Let the comment section become more than reactions.
Let it become a place where wounded people discover they are not the only ones fighting to keep their eyes on Jesus.
The friend who has been drifting.
The brother who laughs whenever Christianity comes up.
The daughter who stopped going to church.
The Christian who looks strong but is quietly unraveling.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
But if this message faithfully points people toward Christ, sharing it can be one practical way of helping another person encounter the truth you believe matters eternally.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is continuing to be challenged, encouraged, corrected, strengthened, and pointed back to Christ.
Even invite the person who doesn't believe any of this yet.
But before you leave, return one last time to Athens.
The Gospel has reached the point where every listener must wrestle with Jesus.
And somewhere in that crowd are Dionysius and Damaris.
But Acts remembers them among those who believed.
Thousands of years later, we still know their names.
Not because they were the loudest people in Athens.
But because when Christ was proclaimed, their response changed.
So what will your response be?
Not the response your Christian friends expect.
Because one day the laughter of every crowd will disappear.
And the question you kept postponing will remain:
What did you do with Jesus Christ?
Athens thought Paul had brought them another strange idea.
And that same Gospel has somehow crossed empires, oceans, languages, persecutions, centuries, and generations until tonight it arrived on the screen in front of you.
Maybe you thought you were simply reading another article.
Maybe God is using it to make you stop running.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
And whatever you do after closing this page...
Do not laugh your way past the empty tomb.
Because the crowd may remember your scandal, but the risen Christ can still rewrite your ending.
